description: We are Hell Boys, a passionate team of developers and innovators participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We are interested in building innovative, software-driven solutions using AI/ML, data science, web development and space technology. Our goal is to solve real-world challenges through creativity, collaboration and technology.
summary:
How can future explorers understand Martian terrain and plan surface journeys when immediate guidance from Earth is unavailable?

MARS EXPLORER is an interactive mapping and mission-planning prototype developed by team Hell Boys for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. It brings terrain exploration, hazard visualization, route planning, historical environmental information and scientific landmarks into one web platform covering Jezero Crater, Gale Crater and Valles Marineris.

The system analyzes regional elevation models to estimate slope and surface roughness, then uses terrain-aware pathfinding to propose routes around modeled obstacles. An optional AI mission copilot explains regional information, while downloadable PDF briefings help users review and share their plans.

NASA mission resources and published planetary research provide scientific context alongside clearly identified reconstructed terrain models and environmental summaries. By connecting geographical information with exploration decisions, MARS EXPLORER helps students, space enthusiasts and researchers understand the challenges of Martian surface travel. It provides a foundation for further mission-planning research, with transparent data limitations and prototype assumptions.
details:
PROJECT OVERVIEW

MARS EXPLORER is an interactive Martian mapping and surface-mission planning prototype developed by team Hell Boys. It addresses the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge by organizing terrain information, environmental context, scientific landmarks and route-planning tools into one accessible platform.

Our project focuses on Jezero Crater, Gale Crater and Valles Marineris. These regions provide different exploration settings, allowing users to investigate crater environments, rover exploration sites and large canyon terrain.

THE PROBLEM

A useful survival map must explain more than where a location is. Explorers also need to understand the terrain between destinations, potential traversal difficulties, available scientific information and the limitations of their maps.

Planetary information is distributed across mission archives, mapping services and scientific publications. MARS EXPLORER brings these resources into a connected workflow that helps users investigate a destination and evaluate a simulated journey.

HOW THE PROJECT WORKS :-

  1. Interactive regional exploration
    Users choose a Martian region and explore its map, landmarks and available information layers. Dedicated views support mission planning, environmental exploration, science observations, hazard analysis and report generation.
  2. Terrain analysis
    The Python backend processes regional elevation models to estimate terrain slope and surface roughness. These derived measurements help distinguish relatively gentle terrain from more difficult areas.

    The geospatial workflow accounts for Martian distances and coordinate conventions. Results depend on the quality and resolution of the underlying regional model.
  3. Hazard visualization
    The system classifies modeled terrain using configurable slope and roughness thresholds. It highlights areas that may require caution or exclusion during route planning.

    These classifications demonstrate how terrain analysis can inform exploration decisions. They are engineering assumptions for the prototype rather than validated astronaut mobility limits.
  4. Terrain-aware route planning
    The route-planning service uses A* and Dijkstra-based search with costs related to distance, slope and surface roughness. Users can investigate how terrain conditions influence a route instead of considering distance alone.

    Travel-time estimates use an adapted walking-speed model. Its application to Martian gravity and spacesuit movement remains an assumption requiring further validation.
  5. Environmental and scientific context
    The platform presents historical environmental summaries associated with Perseverance’s MEDA instrument and Curiosity’s REMS and RAD instruments. Rover observation metadata, landmarks and geological context help users connect their routes with scientific destinations.

    Historical summaries are distinguished from live conditions. Regions without available surface rover observations, including Valles Marineris, are identified accordingly.
  6. AI mission copilot
    An optional Google Gemini integration answers natural-language questions using supplied regional context. When Gemini is unavailable, a rule-based fallback provides responses for supported topics.

    The copilot complements the structured information. It does not independently verify measurements or certify route safety.
  7. Downloadable mission briefings
    The reporting service generates PDF summaries of planning results. These support reviewing, sharing and presenting simulated exploration plans.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT :-

MARS EXPLORER makes planetary information easier to explore and interpret. Students can learn how terrain and environmental conditions influence exploration. Space enthusiasts can investigate mission regions, while researchers and developers can experiment with a modular planning prototype.

Its central benefit is connecting scientific context with geographical decisions. Users can examine a landmark, inspect surrounding terrain, plan a route and review the resulting mission information within one workflow.

The long-term aim is to support further research into accessible planetary planning interfaces. Operational astronaut navigation would require substantially better datasets, verified mobility models and extensive validation.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES:-

Frontend:
React, TypeScript and Vite provide the application structure. Tailwind CSS supports styling, MapLibre GL JS and Cesium support mapping and visualization, Recharts displays charts, and Motion supports interface animations.

Backend:
Python and FastAPI provide the application services. Pydantic supports structured request and response models, while Uvicorn runs the API server.

Geospatial processing:
Rasterio supports raster access. NumPy and SciPy support numerical terrain analysis. PyProj and Shapely support coordinate and geometry operations.

Data and reporting:
GeoTIFF, GeoJSON and JSON organize regional information. A dataset manifest records source references and classifications. ReportLab generates PDF briefings.

AI:
The Google GenAI SDK provides the optional Gemini integration, alongside a local rule-based fallback.

CREATIVITY:-

The project combines an exploratory Mars map with a route-planning workflow and explanatory assistance. Users can move from “What is here?” to “How could we explore it?” while examining the assumptions behind the answer.

Another design priority is separating source observations, reconstructed models and estimates. This helps users understand the confidence they should place in different information layers.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED:-

We considered terrain difficulty, regional data availability, Martian coordinate conventions, historical environmental conditions, usability and dependence on external services.

Core analysis operates on locally stored regional files. Online imagery services and the optional Gemini integration may require connectivity.

DATA LIMITATIONS:-

The current prototype includes reconstructed regional elevation models, imagery proxies and derived geological layers. These should not be interpreted as original high-resolution NASA instrument products.

Environmental summaries are historical rather than real-time weather. Radiation-related spatial estimates use simplified proxies. Terrain resolution limits the ability to represent small obstacles, and the walking-speed model has not been validated for crewed Martian operations.

MARS EXPLORER is an educational and research prototype. Its outputs illustrate planning methods and are not certified navigation or life-safety guidance.

FUTURE DEVELOPMENT:-

Future work includes integrating verified higher-resolution terrain products, improving source traceability, validating route and travel-time estimates, and testing usability with representative mission scenarios.

Additional research directions include rover sensor updates and augmented-reality interfaces. Extending the system to another planetary body would require appropriate datasets, coordinate systems and environmental and mobility models.
